definition: Virulent means extremely severe and destructive in its effects.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word virulent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know virulent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The senator's lead evaporated under a virulent whisper campaign that no denial seemed able to slow.
A mild strain passes through in a day or two and is soon forgotten — the opposite end of the scale from virulent, which kills or cripples what it touches.
Severe goes further than mild — beds fill and recoveries drag — but virulent claims the most: a strain so destructive it kills or cripples swiftly.

Deadly makes one claim and stops: it kills. Virulent grades the whole force of the harm, fatal or not — how hard a disease, a criticism, or a rumor strikes whatever it touches, and how much is destroyed when it does.

Savage describes the manner of an attack — brutal, wild, unrestrained — however much or little damage finally lands. Virulent measures the damage itself: a virulent strain or a virulent rumor is defined by what it destroys, even when it works quietly.

Roman farm manuals used virus for a serpent's venom and for the burning sap of certain plants.
Virulent means extremely severe and destructive in its effects.
Australia loosed the myxoma virus on its rabbit plague in 1950, and the first summer's numbers stunned even the planners: better than ninety-nine of every hundred infected rabbits died.
Nothing in field medicine had seen so virulent an agent.
Within a decade, though, the virus itself had mellowed — versions that killed too fast ran out of hosts to carry them — and virologists still teach the story as virulence negotiating with survival.
Virulent is the exact word for that first summer's virus, because it means extremely severe and destructive in its effects — it grades the force of the blow, not the reach.
A contagious germ spreads easily; an epidemic one has already spread everywhere; a virulent one hits hard, killing or crippling what it touches.
The word travels well, too: criticism and rumors turn virulent when they stop wounding and start destroying.
Virulent grades severity — of pathogens literally, of attacks and rumors by extension — and it always means destructive force, not reach.
Contagious describes spread; deadly counts only the kills.
In this unit it is the adjective among the nouns: a blight or a bane names the destroyer, while virulent tells you how hard it strikes.

In the newspaper wars of the young republic, no weapon was cheaper than a pamphlet.

One 1796 attack on the treasury secretary was so virulent that historians still measure its effects: within a season he lost his allies in the cabinet, his standing in his party, and any hope of higher office.
What is striking is how quietly it worked -- no duels, no riots, just print moving from hand to hand.
Milder squibs of the same year were laughed at over coffee and forgotten by the next post.
The difference, one biographer wrote, was never the anger in the prose; it was the wreckage left behind.
